There is always a way, but first you have to describe in words what
you want the plot to look like.

Here is a starting point. First, I put your data into a data.frame,
and then plotted some of the variables using a combination of colour
and facets.

You can build on this by labelling your variables using descriptive
names (1 and 0 are good for modelling, but not descriptive for
graphing). You can build on this even more by combining some of your
predictors into super-categories. For example, you can combine 'piso'
and 'paredes' into a single variable 'piso.paredes' with four
different levels, and use this combined variable as a faceting
variable.

You might want to look at Prof Harrell's rms package which is a remarkable collection of regression tools reflecting his philosophy, including many graphical displays.

It now (as of V3.0?) produces data frames from the Predict command and these df slide nicely into ggplot2.

Harrell and Hadley are clearly friends and while Harrell's current rms package does not yet make (extensive use) of ggplot, I suspect that plans are afoot.

I will say that have had less success (probably reflecting lack of effort) in converting Harrell's elegant bplot (heat-map) outputs into something equally elegant in ggplot2. But the fautl lies not in the software, but in the operator.  For displaying categorical predictors, etc, you can start with the rms standard outputs and then use the dataframes which get generated by Predict to feed ggplot. That said, rms has a very particular and specific take on things like bootstrapping, calibration, and to use it well really requires engaging with Harrell's larger methodological and statistical perspective.



---------------------------
Robert C James, PhD

You might want to look at Prof Harrell's rms package which is a remarkable collection of regression tools reflecting his philosophy, including many graphical displays.

It now (as of V3.0?) produces data frames from the Predict command and these df slide nicely into ggplot2.

Harrell and Hadley are clearly friends and while Harrell's current rms package does not yet make (extensive use) of ggplot, I suspect that plans are afoot.

I will say that have had less success (probably reflecting lack of effort) in converting Harrell's elegant bplot (heat-map) outputs into something equally elegant in ggplot2. But the fautl lies not in the software, but in the operator.  For displaying categorical predictors, etc, you can start with the rms standard outputs and then use the dataframes which get generated by Predict to feed ggplot. That said, rms has a very particular and specific take on things like bootstrapping, calibration, and to use it well really requires engaging with Harrell's larger methodological and statistical perspective.



---------------------------
Robert C James, PhD

I haven't taken a close look at your data, but the discussion makes me think of fuzzy set analysis. Might be relevant if you can convert your factor levels into set memberships (your dependent is already binary, right?) It gives results in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions which can really help interpretation of different routes to your outcome. Of course if no one knows it in your literature then it's a hard sell. This paper is a good intro:

Fiss PC (2007) A Set-theoretic Approach to Organizational Configurations. Academy of Management Review. 32:1180-1198.

--J

I have done some more work on your graph. Dennis's suggestion can in
fact be simplified a little bit. The following code combines two sets
of factors to display four variables in facets, and uses the fifth as
a categorical variable in the plot itself.

It helps, of course, to understand that the data really is one
variable, with upper and lower confidence limits.

library(ggplot2)

lilu <- paste("iluminacion", 0:1)
lani <- paste("animales", 0:1)
lcie <- paste("cielo.raso", 0:1)
lpis <- paste("piso", 0:1)
lpar <- paste("paredes", 0:1)

d$iluminacion <- as.factor(lilu[d$iluminacion + 1])
d$animales <- as.factor(lani[d$animales + 1])
d$cielo.raso <- as.factor(lcie[d$cielo.raso +1])
d$piso <- as.factor(lpis[d$piso + 1])
d$paredes <- as.factor(lpar[d$paredes + 1])

d$factor1 <- paste(d$animales, d$cielo.raso)
d$factor2 <- paste(d$piso, d$paredes)

p <- ggplot(d, aes(x=iluminacion)) +
facet_grid(factor1~factor2) +
geom_point(aes(y=condicion)) +
geom_linerange(aes(ymin=lcl, ymax=ucl))
print(p)

---

Andrie
